title: Why You Should Stop Using Video To Teach
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Recounting a formal classroom observation, Linsin describes watching a teacher let an animated video carry an entire lesson on three-dimensional shapes while several boys visibly disengaged — melting into their seats as if hit with tranquilizer darts — and later learning those same boys were being considered for behavioral interventions and testing for attention disorders. His central claim is that this misdiagnosis has the causality backwards: the boredom and inattention weren't evidence of a disorder, they were a predictable response to passive, outsourced instruction. He argues that delivering compelling lessons in person is the second, equally non-negotiable half of classroom management, alongside behavior management itself, and that leaning on video, self-directed programs, or other proxies for direct teaching does real damage to students who need to be moved, challenged, and captivated. The concrete recommendation is to sharply limit video and self-learning modes in favor of live storytelling, modeling, and expert-driven instruction. He closes by putting responsibility squarely on the teacher: if classroom management is solid but students are still bored, the problem is the lesson, not the students.
